agentes-de-ia-en-produccion.title: AI agents in production: what changes between the demo and everyday use
agentes-de-ia-en-produccion.excerpt: An AI demo wins people over in an afternoon. Making it work every day with real data is a different job: connections, logs, limits and a person who reviews.
agentes-de-ia-en-produccion.body:
An AI agent demo comes together in an afternoon: a chat that answers from the company's documents or summarizes the day's email. Everyone is convinced. The trouble starts later, when it has to work with real data, every day, without anyone watching.

Real data. In the demo, the agent reads three tidy PDFs. In everyday use, it reads the company's system: orders, customers, inventory. It has to be connected to the source, with permissions, and someone has to decide what it can and can't read.

A log of every answer. Each time the agent replies or does something, it records what it received, what it looked up and what it returned. Without that, when something goes wrong there is no way to know why.

Clear limits. An agent that looks things up is not the same as one that acts. If it is going to send an email, change an order or charge a card, the sensible start is for it to propose and a person to approve, widening its permissions over time.

When to hand off to a person. Some questions aren't its job: a complaint, an odd case, an upset customer. The agent has to recognize them and pass them to someone on the team, with all the context.

Measure. How many queries it solved on its own, how many it handed off, how long it took and what each one costs. Those numbers decide whether the agent stays, gets adjusted or gets switched off.

Start with a single process. The most common mistake is wanting one agent that does everything. It works better to pick a repetitive, measurable task, such as answering order status, sorting incoming email or reading supplier invoices, and do it well.

The least glamorous part takes the most work: connecting systems. At Feniz, for example, MetaTrader 5 offered no way to get trades out, so we wrote a program that runs inside the platform and sends them every five seconds. Agents are no different: the AI is one piece, and what makes it useful is everything around it.

facturacion-electronica-tienda-online.title: E-invoicing in your online store: what to sort out before you start selling
facturacion-electronica-tienda-online.excerpt: Receipts, invoices and credit notes that go out with every sale, without copying orders into another system. What to ask of your store so the receipt isn't a separate job.
facturacion-electronica-tienda-online.body:
In Peru, almost every business that sells issues electronic receipts: a boleta when the customer is a person, a factura when they buy with a RUC tax ID, and a credit note when something has to be refunded or corrected. In an online store the problem usually isn't issuing them, but that they are issued in another system: someone copies the store's orders into the invoicing tool, by hand, at the end of the day.

That manual step brings the usual errors: totals that don't match, a mistyped RUC, forgotten receipts and an inventory that no longer matches what was sold. And it grows with sales: with ten orders a day it's bearable; with a hundred, someone spends the afternoon copying.

The receipt goes out with the sale. When payment is confirmed, the store builds the boleta or factura from the order data and sends it to SUNAT, directly or through an OSE, without anyone typing it again.

The customer chooses at checkout. Boleta or factura is decided before paying, and the RUC is validated right then, not when it already needs fixing.

The receipt arrives and stays on file. The customer gets it by email with its PDF and XML, and it stays attached to the order for whenever it has to be found.

Refunds close themselves. The credit note is issued from the same order and the stock goes back where it was.

One catalog for the website and the shop. If a product sells at the till, it stops showing as available online, and the other way around.

This isn't theory. In Vendiq, the commerce software we build and run, a sale in the demo store goes from end to end without anyone stepping in: stock is deducted, the receipt is issued, SUNAT accepts it, and only then is the shipment prepared.

If you invoice your online sales by hand today, the first step isn't switching stores: it's measuring how much time goes into copying orders and how many errors come from it. With that number, the decision is easy.

antes-de-publicar-tu-web.title: Before you publish your website: what the law and Google will ask of you
antes-de-publicar-tu-web.excerpt: A complaints book, a privacy policy, a visible tax ID, cookies that wait for consent and the basics for Google to find you. The list we go through before every launch.
antes-de-publicar-tu-web.body:
A new website is usually reviewed for how it looks. But there is another, less visible list that, if missing, brings fines or keeps the site out of Google. It's the one we go through before every launch. The legal points below apply in Peru.

Complaints book. If you serve the public, and an online store or a services website does, you need a virtual libro de reclamaciones. It has to be in plain sight, less than two clicks from the home page: a link in the footer works. And it has to be a real form that lets people choose between a claim and a complaint, not a notice saying it exists.

Tax ID and business details. Your RUC and legal name must appear on the website, together with an address, a phone number and an email. The footer is the natural place for all four.

Privacy policy. A contact form already collects personal data, so Law 29733 applies. The policy has to say who is responsible, what data is collected and why, how long it is kept and how to ask for it to be corrected or deleted, with an email address someone actually reads.

Cookies with consent. Analytics and ad pixels shouldn't load before the person accepts. A notice that appears after the cookies are already set doesn't do its job, and continuing to browse is not the same as accepting.

Terms and conditions. If you sell, they are the contract: returns, delivery times, warranties and support channels.

What Google asks for. Its own title and description on every page, a sitemap, a robots.txt that doesn't block what matters, the image that shows up when someone shares the link, and the canonical address. Without them, the site exists but is hard to find.

The technical things nobody sees. HTTPS on every page, images sized right so it loads fast on a phone, backups, and someone who gets the alert if the site goes down.

None of this is hard to do while the site is being built; what's expensive is finding out it was missing once the notice has arrived. If your website is already live, it's worth going through this list once.

transformacion-digital.title: How digital transformation accelerates your business
transformacion-digital.excerpt: Keys to prioritizing digital initiatives that deliver real impact on operations and customer experience.
transformacion-digital.body:
Digital transformation is not just technology: it's rethinking processes, culture and customer experience with a focus on measurable results. In this article we look at how to prioritize initiatives that deliver real impact on operations and your relationship with users.

Starting with a clear assessment of digital maturity helps identify quick wins and strategic projects for the medium term. Alignment between business, product and technology is essential for investments to turn into sustainable competitive advantages.

In practice, many companies start by automating repetitive processes —document management, billing, inventory— and then move on to digital sales and customer service channels. Order matters: tackling what frees up operational capacity first usually delivers the fastest return.

Digital customer experience is another pillar: a well-designed website or app not only attracts users, but reduces support costs and creates data that enables continuous improvement of products and services.

metodologias-agiles.title: Agile methodologies in software projects
metodologias-agiles.excerpt: Why Scrum and Kanban aren't just for technical teams: measurable benefits in timelines, quality and business alignment.
metodologias-agiles.body:
Scrum, Kanban and agile practices aren't exclusive to development teams: they help any team deliver value iteratively, with visibility and the ability to adjust constantly.

In software projects, applying well-understood agile frameworks improves timelines, quality and alignment with the business. The key is adapting the framework to the reality of the team and the organization, not following ceremonies by inertia.

Short sprints of two or three weeks enable early feedback and course correction without major waste. Daily standups, retrospectives and a prioritized backlog create a rhythm that avoids the "big bang" at the end of the project.

When business and technology work together from the start —with clear user stories, acceptance criteria and frequent demos— the outcome tends to better match what the market actually needs.

ia-en-el-negocio.title: Artificial intelligence applied to business
ia-en-el-negocio.excerpt: From process automation to conversational agents: concrete use cases and how to start with an MVP.
ia-en-el-negocio.body:
Artificial intelligence opens possibilities from automating repetitive tasks to conversational agents and recommendation systems. To leverage it without spreading efforts thin, it helps to identify concrete use cases with measurable impact.

Starting with a focused MVP —for example, a chatbot for frequent queries or an assistant to summarize documents— lets you validate value and complexity before scaling. The combination of quality data, suitable models and integration with existing systems often makes the difference between a successful pilot and one that never takes off.

LLMs (large language models) have made it easier to access capabilities such as text analysis, content generation and conversational response. Integrating them via APIs with your current flows —CRM, email, knowledge base— is a practical starting point.

Defining clear metrics from the start —time saved, user satisfaction, resolution rate— helps assess whether the pilot is worth it and which direction to scale.
